items.excerpt: Senegalese singer Fania Niang has been making noteworthy music for over two decades. items.body: Ivo Perelman is a musician, artist, and jeweller who works with many musicians of different styles. He sees the world slightly differently from some of us, in that he sees sound in colour. So the title of the recording, Synesthesia , is apt. In his contribution to my book Music Is Your Superpower , Perelman describes music not as a choice, but as an essential for existence. He says of music, and jazz in particular, “What truly connected me to jazz was the emotional intensity within its structure, especially in the music of Shorter. It felt almost impossible to perform music that was so intricately constructed while simultaneously conveying such depth of feeling.” He also talks about his synesthesia – the phenomenon of seeing sound as colours. When Perelman plays music, it feels as if he is creating a work of art, and when he is painting, he can relate it to creating a saxophone solo. Art, colour, and music are interlinked. His intense need to create may explain his productivity in music. His way of playing and interpreting musical dialogue draws to him musicians who understand his musical visions. On Synesthesia , Perelman has teamed again with close associates Matthew Shipp (piano), William Parker (bass), and Bobby Kapp (drums) in a new recording that captures their deep connection and still evolving voices in contemporary free jazz. With the pathways forged with ‘Ineffable Joy’ and ‘Heptagon’, the group continues to establish new routes in spontaneous composition, open form, and strong collective interplay. The difference on ‘Synesthesia’ is that the music is more crystallised, and has a deeper sense of flow and connection. That connection is revealed in the rapid reactions of the musicians as they listen and respond to each other, offering individual takes that go to create a whole. Perelman explores his tenor sax, moving across its range with soft, melodic interludes, intense, electric solos, and contrasting altissimo. Shipp demonstrates his innate art of support as his circling, looping chordal progressions offer up subtle melodic ideas that pilot the ensemble in places. The bass of Parker is constant, with deep, sonorous melodies, with space left for musical dialogue. Kapp adds colour and motion, while filling in the detail of the sonic landscape with percussive touches and occasional solos. Across the album, there is that contrast of intense energy, such as on ‘First Color Heard,’ and quiet, reflective passages, such as those on ‘Afterglow.’ The contrasts coexist, interlinked and cohesive to create the harmonic dialogue that only comes with experience and understanding other musicians. On ‘Phosphene,’ Perelman travels familiar pathways, yet introduces new elements into each, creating a sense of the unexpected. Shipp’s piano excels on this track with its quiet support and triumphantly emergent solo work. The beautiful moment when Perelman enters across the piano solo with astonishingly accurate pitch contrast is just beautiful. There is even a snippet from a song from Perelman before he reverts to free playing. Into the quiet moments, Parker’s bass sighs and works its magic – an excellent track. On ‘Blue Taste,’ the influence of jazz masters past and present can be felt as the ensemble delivers free-style jazz commentary across a blues-infused rhythm pattern. Perelman's pipping, and squealing contrast with the steadfast whirr of the accompaniment, while ‘Afterglow’ is a much gentler affair altogether. ‘One Sense’ has an atmosphere of a ‘50s jazz venue for some inexplicable reason, possibly because of the interaction between traditional rhythms and free playing – glorious. Like in a lot of Perelman’s work, the blues and bop elements make themselves known, interwoven amidst abstract sonic textures that create a flowing, organic development. Synesthesia is a recording that has the quality you might expect from an experienced ensemble, who know each other’s ways so well, yet it still has elements of surprise and supreme intuitive styling that give it its energy and expression. On Synesthesia , there is no discernible fixed structure, yet the harmonics and classically linked progressions tell of a musical ensemble deeply knowledgeable in musical scaffolding and pinning on that scaffold experimental lines that always work back to the root. The title says it all, a kaleidoscope of jewelled, colourful music, with deep, dark textures and light, contrasting hues. There are shapes woven here, along with colorful landscapes, through which the ensemble meanders, careens, and gently rests on occasion. This is an album that will have broad appeal. Olivia Rodrigo has officially released her third studio album, you seem pretty sad for a girl so in love, via Geffen Records. The 13-track record follows the massive success of SOUR and GUTS, and arrives alongside the official music video for album cut 'stupid song'.

Directed by Mitch Ryan and filmed in New York City, the visual stars New York City Ballet principal dancer Tiler Peck alongside performers from the New York City Ballet and American Ballet Theatre. The choreography-driven clip offers a theatrical accompaniment to one of the album's standout tracks.

The new album is split into two thematic halves — girl so in love and you seem pretty sad — and features previously released singles 'drop dead' and 'the cure'. The former made chart history by making Rodrigo the first artist to debut the lead singles from her first three albums at No. 1, while 'the cure' topped multiple Billboard alternative charts upon release.

Rodrigo has also been celebrating a string of major career milestones in recent months. In May, she appeared at Spotify's Billions Club Live after becoming one of the platform's most-streamed artists, with nine songs surpassing one billion streams. She also surprised fans at Primavera Sound with a live debut of 'what's wrong with me', featuring Robert Smith of The Cure.

The album arrives ahead of The Unraveled Tour, which kicks off in September. The global trek has already sold more than one million tickets and added multiple dates across North America and Europe due to overwhelming demand. Notable stops include 10 nights at Los Angeles' Intuit Dome, a 10-show residency at Brooklyn's Barclays Center, and 11 performances at London's The O2.

items.body:
Fans are getting a rare glimpse of YEONJUN beyond the spotlight. Running from 12 June to 21 June, Yeonjun by Petra Collins with VOGUE SALON sees the TOMORROW X TOGETHER star collaborate with acclaimed photographer and artist Petra Collins for a special exhibition presented in partnership with Vogue Korea.

Known for her dreamlike visual language and intimate portraiture, Collins turns her lens toward one of K-pop's most recognisable performers, capturing a side of YEONJUN that fans rarely get to see. The exhibition features around 90 works that explore the contrasts that define the artist both on and off stage.

Rather than focusing on elaborate concepts or performance-driven imagery, the collection highlights subtle expressions, fleeting moments, and the quiet magnetism that has made YEONJUN a standout figure in music and fashion. Through Collins' perspective, visitors are invited into a more personal portrait of the artist, one that balances innocence, confidence, and allure.

Speaking about the project, YEONJUN shared, “I have always admired Petra Collins’ work, but I could never quite imagine what I would look like inside her frame. That’s why I was so looking forward to this project.”

He added, “Although I’m very used to being in front of the camera, this project brought out a whole new version of myself. It was fascinating to see myself in a completely different light.”

Collins also reflected on the experience, saying, “Shooting YEONJUN was such a pleasure. Since the moment I met him, he’s been incredibly kind, curious, and full of life. There’s a warmth and openness to him that makes being around him feel effortless.”

The exhibition arrives amid a busy period for YEONJUN, who continues to expand his influence beyond music. Following his solo debut with 'GGUM', the artist released his first solo album, NO LABELS: PART 01, which debuted at No. 10 on the Billboard 200. He was also recently announced as a Friend of the House for Miu Miu.

items.body: The concept of virtuosity is often misunderstood as an outsized display of technique. In truth though, by definition and in reality, it's about mastery. Such expertise is just as likely to be shown in measured command as it is to appear as fireworks, and this absorbing duo date is a firm reminder of that fact. Legendary bassist Ron Carter and eminent guitarist Yotam Silberstein each possess extraordinary skills and have the wisdom and experience to know when not to flaunt them. That balance between sparkle and spare elegance is what makes Duets such a delight to behold. Crafted in part as a tribute to the late Jim Hall and a nod to the Carter-Hall partnership—and recorded, by divine coincidence, on Hall's birthday—this music, nevertheless, speaks to its own creative duo-logue. Across eight performances, Carter and Silberstein traverse styles, language and states of being. Opening on "Nova Ilusão," this pair demonstrates the draw of a gentle Brazilian sway. Carter's work is supportively buoyant, his note choices providing better direction than any compass could, and Silberstein's melodic suggestions and flourishes mesh beautifully with his low-end companion's perfectly placed lines. "Love Letter" swings and sings brighter than many a take on that Victor Young and Edward Heyman classic. Carter delivers a walk to remember, Silberstein shines with both single note splendors and quality chording, and all is right and tight in the flow. Two Silberstein tunes—the album's only originals—follow that opening diptych and prove complementary. "Blues for Brother Malone," dedicated to noted guitarist Russell Malone, a longtime member of Carter's musical circle who passed away while on tour with the bassist in 2024, lives in the composer's and honoree's shared wheelhouse. Tempo and tone are all about downhome sophistication, a "Sonnymoon for Two" quote serves as the baton handoff between solos, and an earthy grace prevails at every turn. "Rain Again," in a different vein, is purity in precipitation and conversational blend. "The Lamp is Low," born in the '30s and bound to Ravel-ian influence, offers energy without ego. Both musicians find a swinging stride and pace each other throughout. Vernon Duke and Yip Harburg's "What Is There To Say?," another standard drawn from the same era, is firm finesse close to the heart. In both tracks/cases, Carter and Silberstein captivate by finding something new to say in the most well-worn of settings. Irving Berlin's "They Say It's Wonderful," in penultimate placement, unfolds with sprightly significance, reflecting its own aura and optimism through singing strings. Then it's a bop-leaning bon voyage in the form of tenor saxophone slinger Johnny Griffin's "Mil Dew." A lively and interactive exit, this performance affirms what can be heard all across Duets—virtuosity in its truest form.

items.body: Atmospheric does not begin to describe Filipa Santos and Miguel Moreira's recording Now Swim. The music emits from another dimension, a soundtrack from the bottom of the ocean: exotic and dense, weird and abrasive, soothing and lulling, often simultaneously. Santos' saxophone, flute and voice are often unearthly, being manipulated electronically and creating an eerie, ghostly presence. Moreira's guitar and percussion programming vary from providing a deep rhythm to creating a cacophony of noise that explodes in the middle of a song. It is an album best listened to from start to finish as the songs merge and build on each other. For example, going from "Float"—which sounds like its name, airy and light—to "Bridge," which starts slowly and abstractly, building to Moreira unleashing his guitar in joyous feedback before slowing back down, to the driving rhythm of "Cosmic Ship," all which feels like an unexpected journey to the cosmos, Santos' sax leading the way through the electronic blips and guitar drones. The Portuguese duo have released two albums previously, but Now Swim is their most accomplished work. The liner notes suggest a philosophical approach to the music that is implicit in the title: "Swimming implies accepting instability. It implies trusting the environment that sustains without offering fixed ground." And it is the exploratory nature of the improvisation they employ that makes the album so fascinating. Often, the listener might not even be sure what instrument is being played. What sounds like a kalimba on "Limnology" could be a guitar being plucked, a synthesizer or electronically manipulated sounds. Or all of the above. The synchronicity between the two musicians is immense, each driving the other until a song builds to an unexpected climax, like they are finishing each other's dreams. Now Swim is a compelling album, full of beauty and strangeness, so dive right in.

items.body: Chicago-based trumpeter and composer Rich Willey oversees an impressive eleven-piece ensemble on Best Laid Plans, which embodies seven of his melodically enticing and rhythmically strong compositions, all neatly arranged by Wally Minko. The one clear drawback in this otherwise pleasing session, however, is an incessant rock beat, which lends an aura of sameness to every number that serves to weaken its purpose and impede even the most valiant efforts to separate it from the herd. That is countered to some extent by the inclusion of John Swana's EVI (electric valve instrument), whose unique solo voice adds welcome variety on most tracks. On balance, however, the EVI, even though invigorating, is unable to neutralize the adverse effects of the constant and repetitive drumbeat. Once past that, the music is by and large admirable: engaging melodies, well-drawn charts, forceful blowing by the ensemble, earnest solos by Willey, Swana, pianist (and organist) Paul Mutzabaugh, trombonist Steve Duncan and soprano saxophonist Jim Gailloretto. Willey composed every song including "That's My Little Girl," the lone exception to the funky two-beat format. He and Swana are especially impressive on "Long Lost Brothers," sharing the melodic chores before trading elegant solos. Mutzabaugh solos there too, as he does (on Hammond) on the frisky opener, "Laid Back," and (electric) piano on "My Little Girl." Swana is suitably bracing and ethereal whenever he solos, which is on five of the album's seven numbers; he sits out only on the well-named "Relax & Take It Easy" and similarly even-tenpered "Ladies First." The rhythm section is fine, and one can hardly blame drummer Charles Heath for the annoying drum play; he was only doing what was asked of him. On balance, a well-above-average session whose many charming moments far outweigh the ill-advised choice to set most of them to undue and less-than-engaging rhythms. Earnestly recommended for its many positive aspects.

items.body: Krokofant is a Norwegian trio formed in 2011, built around the combustible chemistry of Tom Hasslan on guitar, Jorgen Mathisen on saxophone and synthesizers, and Axel Skalstad on drums. After two albums as a five-piece, they stripped back to their original trio format for 6, and the results are formidable. "Oh My God" announces itself immediately. A striking and melodic unison hook shifts across registers, giving the track a bold, gripping energy that does not let up. The synergistic interplay between all three players is at the heart of everything here; this is a band that listens as fiercely as it plays. Hasslan's solo moves through psychedelic and prog-rock territory with real conviction before transitioning seamlessly into fluid jazz stylizations and delicious harmonies, with the shift feeling entirely natural rather than forced. At different points in time, a lurking undercurrent of sound shadows the foreground, subtly altering the atmosphere and creating space for Hasslan's most expressive playing. The trio tears it up with the same fierce ambition that drives the album as a whole, before circling back to revisit the opening complex theme at the closeout—a satisfying and compositionally astute resolution. Nonetheless, few bands working in jazz-rock today match Krokofant's ability to balance raw improvisational energy with sharp compositional thinking.

items.body:
You'd be forgiven for thinking horsegiirL was some kind of joke. Blame it on mortal prejudice, but it's easy to see an equine humanoid making waves in club culture and write it off as performance art. The evidence certainly skews in that direction: in 2022, first, there was the  breakthrough set  where she wore a tank top emblazoned with the slogan (confession?) "I am a horse, not a DJ," swiftly followed by viral TikTok stormer " My Barn, My Rules. " Since then, countless buzzy  interviews  winking through the screen. For a project so balled up in spectacle, horsegiirL's ascendancy has almost been hijacked by the reams of internet discourse.

Almost.  Nature Is Healing , her debut album, puts to rest any notion that Stella Stallion (AKA horsegiirL) is a clickbaity troll or one-note stunt. This is a full-length of consummate musicianship, interpolating decades' worth of Eurotrash, heavy techno and glossy pop into a rich, oaty feed. For an unstuffy listener with a predilection for something  fun , the album of the summer is here. 

Working with a stable that includes A.G. Cook, Casey MQ, Margo XS, and Nomak—producers whose combined resumes boast the likes of  Charli xcx ,  Oklou , and Kim Petras—means that  Nature Is Healing  sounds expensive. This pedigree might also have you believe that this is going to be a classic hyperpop party, and at first, it seems like that. The queasy, helium-laced, sing-song taunts of album-opener "351%" ("If I was a symphony, it would be a bop") gives way to the controlled-chaos cacophony of "that's my beach!" a paean to tan lines and shaking ass which alternates between music-box keyboard lines and skull-crushing synths with a few dolphin barks thrown in for good measure.

After the hyperpop of its opening one-two punch,  Nature Is Healing  switches up. There's  the breezy Eurodance of "hands hands hands," with an accordion line that immediately transports you to the heyday of late 2000s chart-toppers; the saxophone-heavy "connect the dots," which stays  just  on the right side of cheesy and is easy to imagine blasting out of open windows on long coastal drives for years to come; as well as "only the best," which comes off like Kylie Minogue with a knack for panpipe solos. A few tracks later, she canters to another field entirely, with the '90s-throwback, R&B-esque saxophone over excoriations of a lover stealing her heart. 

This cornucopia of genre references might make for whiplash, but this isn't her first rodeo. But this also gets to the heart of the horsegiirL paradox: she is so defined as being of the moment, that it can be hard to imagine her record having staying power beyond our current zeitgeist. Does the lower energy on "rivers run free" really add that much to the current trip hop revival, for example? Will future generations really chime with the Zoomer overdrive of "AURA?"

But horsegiirL's staying power emerges when she shows off her wide, varied knowledge of dance music. Take "an apple a day," which starts out as an old-school  electroclash  barnburner, campily rapping the varieties of apples before morphing into a frenetic gabber stomper, mixing in the crunch of an apple and a freakishly-paced piano line into its soundboard. In this skull-crushing climax, a vocoded robot voice intones "I'm so angry, I'm the doctor. No one needs me, I'm the doctor." The joke speaks for itself.

Suffice to say,  Nature Is Healing  is a good-times album, a pleasuredome of hedonist joy. Yet expectations that will enrage as much as it delights are wide of the mark. While she might not take herself too seriously–oftentimes the ecstasy of a dance floor is all the message you need—these are still serious works of contemporary, dance floor-angled pop. When the strobes cool down, you might even have the balladry of the title track ringing in your ear. Over a web of downtempo drums and chill out room field recordings, horsegiirL delivers an affecting mission statement: "I just want to dedicate this song to every single creature, every plant, every little bug on this beautiful big planet. You're amazing." Winking, perhaps. Earnest, undeniably.

items.body:
Our radio station project, 9128.live is still alive and kicking. Crazy to think it’s been 6 years now since we launched. I recently stumbled into someone at a show who was with us for our all-weekend takeovers during the pandemic era, and he said it helped him get through one of the hardest times of his life. It was very humbling to hear, and despite rarely hearing these comments, it’s one of the reasons I still keep this thing alive. 

 I’m quietly updating music in the background on the station - of course, ASIP music is easy for me to keep updated in rotation, and a few other labels keep on top of things with new releases. without much fanfare. 

 Here are a few key updates that you might have missed: 

 New label partners 

 In the past year or so, we’ve added three amazing catalogs into rotation, including Quiet Details (just this week), Never Late, and Analog Attic. Between these 3 labels alone, we’re hosting some of the most majestic music to hit our ears in recent years. I’m also adding some one-off artist music into rotation, as some listeners get in touch with their own music that fits. 

 Memberships 

 We had a membership that enabled paying users to access unreleased and exclusive sets. I let this dwindle for far too long, so I’m sorry to anyone who kept going with it. But I’ve now canceled it fully as I don’t see the time or space to make this worthwhile right now. Thank you to everyone who helped us keep the station going with their contributions. 

 Listening apps 

 Not new news, but very importantly, we have both iOS and Android apps that enable you to listen to the stream, and they also host the isolatedmix series as a podcast too. A few other bells and whistles to check out too. Links to the apps here. 

 Sonos 

 One of my favorite ways to listen is actually through Sonos (at night) and it’s not too easy to make that happen. But essentially, you need to add the stations custom listen URL into your TuneIn app (once downloaded), then add the TuneIn Service to Sonos, and it should then show in your faves. See here for more ways to listen. 

 The 9128 label 

 When we had regular weekend takeovers, artists were preparing sets for their slots, many of which were original, so we decided to release some of these sets and begin the label. Check out the releases here , by Jo Johnson & Hilary Robinson, Gailes, 36 and Ameeva. With no pipeline for original releases, the label is on a bit of a hiatus, but I hope to spin this up again one day and may open up the catalog to live releases in general. 

 The future 

 Being transparent, the radio costs thousands of dollars to run and host each year. For now, it’s an investment and a bit of a vanity project because I use it so much myself. So a big thank you to everyone who donates to help with this cost. I hope I get to spend more time on the project in the near future, and bring back proper programming and weekend takeovers again. Until then, I’m doing my best to keep the lights on and keeping 24/7 ambient and electronic music flowing.

items.body: Gabriel Vicéns first came to my attention with 2024’s Mural , which itself was a big step in the young guitarist and composer’s musical evolution. That album marked a turn from the Latin-tinged modern jazz of his previous work toward modernist and postmodernist classical traditions. Niebla finds Vicéns with a sextet with whom he has years of history, but, as far as I can tell, has never stretched so far into this blended, abstract musical territory, at least together. The crew includes saxophonist Roman Filiú, pianist Vitor Gonçalves, bassist Rick Rosato, and the double percussion section of E.J Strickland and Victor Pablo, in addition to Vicéns himself on guitar. On Niebla (fog), Vicéns and crew simultaneously take a step further out and a step back to Caribbean traditions. For some a split like this would tear at the ligaments of conviction. Here, the group shows rare agility in pulling it off. The album has a lot going for it. Influences range from contemporary jazz to especially Feldman and Cage-inspired classical to Puerto Rican and Cuban rhythmacism. Now, new music and driving rhythm may seem anathema to each other. Throw in some jumpy bop lines (I cannot shake the feeling that some of these phrases are slightly laggard takes on Salt Peanuts, or something like it), Filiú’s and Vicéns entangling lines (I hear nods to Metheny in the latter), Gonçalves’ seasoned restraint, and a wildly pulsing rhythm section and one might think the resulting stew could never settle properly. But it does. The jauntier fusion numbers here – Niebla, Stray Dogs – lay into that kaleidoscopic description above. The more patient pieces – 900-50-80, Guaiza – strike an unexpectedly convincing balance between repetition, abstraction, and gradualism. The odd time signatures and especially the polyrhythmic drumming add to this, hinting at phasing and free jazz arrhythmia. So too do the moments when the band spans the gap between old and new, or indigenous and hypermodernist practices, as in the scratchy güiro solo about nine minutes into the vertiginous Ramaje. This one runs from some Escherian hive of staircases to noirish jazz (with a solo by Strickland worthy of Andrew Cyrille) to straight-up New York minimalism to the barest of güiro scrapes and rasps framed by silence, or, as the listener’s ears remain perked, an aural fog of what preceded and anticipation of what might come next. In that, Niebla is liminal, resting on the boundary between traditions and, in its various twists and turns, eschewing complacency in any given moment or direction. items.body: Some guys have all the luck, and Zev Feldman is a lucky guy. Imagine criss-crossing the world on a rogue yet holy mission to bring the music all back home, and listening to, for the first time, works of art as snazzy or as regal as "Up Jumped Spring," the second of six tracks on CD1 of the 2-CD / 2-LP set, So Many Lovely Things: Live in Brecon. Jazz has known its shamans: those few who roam among us, going toe-to-toe with the blues. And then there is Kenny Barron. A gentle man from all accounts, Barron has been the fulcrum where side one becomes side two and forward goes the torch. That his touch is touched by grace makes for a smooth handoff made even smoother with both bassist supremo Ray Drummond and the much-decorated Ben Riley on drums in the house. And they are as pumped to get a jump on things as their pianist is, as "Oh, Look At Me Now," a certified chestnut back in 1995, and "Up Jumped Spring"'s immediate predecessor, blithely attest. In these six hands—do the math: two hands per person times three—So Many Lovely Things: Live in Brecon becomes the smooth, rare gem all musicians strive to cut. Like any human endeavor, there is a backstory, and collaboration is key. So just imagine as Barron, a man of humor and wisdom, Drummond, with his teacherly side, and Riley, Thelonious Monk's wing man, welcome in all 475 folk, thus packing the Brycheiniog Theatre on the grounds of the Brecon Jazz Festival, Wales ca. 1995, and create an evening of magic, of movement, and happy memory. Still in the baby years of their roughly 15-year trio run, Barron, Drummond, and Riley start on a high and ride the waves as So Many Lovely Things: Live in Brecon crests and crests with "Surrey With the Fringe On Top" and all its firework pace and popping groove. The romanticism of "Silent Rain." Eighteen minutes of Monk jauntily transpire in the solo highlight "Shuffle Boil" and harmonically revealing "Ask Me Why." Produced by Feldman and veteran Spanish promoter Jordi Suñol from original recordings housed in the Jordi Suñol Archives, So Many Lovely Things: Live in Brecon is another feather in the cap of everyone involved.

"Everyone must understand their role and come prepared by doing the hard work of study and practice," he said. "Each person will get to say their piece, but it is in the act of integrating as a band that the musicians ultimately create something bigger, richer, and deeper." Oracles launches into a time and place where divisions are deep and democracy is under attack, which makes it a perfect moment to reflect on and embrace Heath's view. As her first big-band offering, the album is Sung's response—to Heath and Clark Terry, Ron Carter, Wayne Shorter, Barry Harris, Kenny Barron, Herbie Hancock, and Sir Roland Hanna—which, as she put it, "expresses my deep gratitude and is a tribute to the masters who made room for me and entrusted me with a tradition they helped build." Her compositions affirm lessons she has learned and values she has internalized. In "A Little Bird Watchin' (for Jimmy Heath)," the ensemble leads the way. What begins with one voice (Nicole Glover's tenor saxophone) quickly becomes lively counterpoint as independent lines are layered in, followed by full-voiced harmonious homophony. Improvisation is the order of the day, with Vicente Archer's bass, Sung's piano, and Adam Cruz's drums coming to the fore as textures and tempos shift. Soloists dominate. There is plenty of composition, but it serves and is led by individual voices (those of "the people," to use Heath's metaphor). Taking Ron Carter's advice to heart, that "in order to find your voice in this music, you have to write your own music," she uses material by her mentors as jumping-off points for creations that are very much her own. Terry's "Samba da Gumz" (track 2) becomes a prelude to her "Positively C.T." (track 3), which highlights her trumpets (Mike Rodriguez, Tatum Greenblatt, Alex Norris, Nathaniel Williford). And Shorter's gorgeous "Diana" (track 4), which Shorter so memorably offered in his 1974 collaboration with Milton Nascimento (Native Dancer, Columbia), here becomes a dreamy prelude for soprano sax (John Ellis) and Fender Rhodes, leading to Sung's quixotic "Wayne's World" (track 5). Sung's "Mr. Virtuoso" (track 6), written for Carter, opens with bass, piano, and drums in an out-of-time misterioso before she employs the full range of the ensemble, from flutes on top to the lower realms of her reed and brass sections. She plumbs the depths with solos from Andrew Gutauskas' baritone saxophone and Gina Benalcázar López's bass trombone then uses Carter's own "R.J." as a postlude, picking up the tempo and again centering on the rhythm section. Sung followed Hanna's counsel to "not forget her classical roots" in composing Pianism, a piano concerto in tribute to Harris, Barron, and Hancock. The first movement, "I: Barry Harris," opens with a non-blues pentatonic passage in parallel harmony that is gradually reshaped metrically against a changing set of backdrops, finally settling—two minutes into the performance—into a bop melodic, rhythmic, and harmonic milieu reflective of Harris' position as "keeper of Bud Powell's legacy and the bebop flame." The timbres soften in the second movement, "II: Kenny Barron," which honors the "modern master of melody" with Rhodes, flute, and muted trumpet lines that sail on a cool groove that navigates swing and straight eighths. "III: Herbie Hancock," comes on strong with percussion hits and horns in a pentatonic canon that recalls the concerto's opening while heralding a funkier feel with a finely calibrated 16th-note subdivision and blues mode in its melodic backbone. In keeping with her view of Hancock as "transcendence personified," Sung closes the concerto with a finale that aligns conceptually with aesthetic and formal norms of classical composition. She reminds us who and what we have heard in earlier movements, recapping themes, playing with and intertwining elements, transcending stylistic boundaries to create a work that—while it respects the "without you, no me" jazz principle—is undeniably, joyfully original.

items.body: Pianist and composer Alexander Hawkins has spent years at the forefront of the European jazz avant- garde scene, leading various mutations of the standard group format, from solo piano to large ensembles and everything in between. Experimenting with different dynamics, instruments, and musicians, and adapting them to fulfill the needs of the music has been his calling card for nearly two decades now. On No Nation But Imagination, Hawkins once again mixes things up, putting together a unique lineup featuring piano, flute, harp, drums, synthesizers, samplers, and turntables. This new quintet is a juxtaposition of electronic and acoustic instrumentation, and this mix creates a harmonic and structural friction integral to the music they play, almost as if the group is an instrument itself. Flutist Nicole Mitchell and drummer Hamid Drake, who are both firmly grounded in the Chicago sounds of the AACM, establish the living pulse of the music. However, this pulse is challenged by both the harp of Rhodri Davies and the samples and digital manipulations of Matthew Wright. Firmly woven into the songs' structure, these elements give the proceedings a futuristic, alien feel, as if beamed in from another galaxy. Also interesting is that Hawkins's piano rarely takes the lead; it is often Davies who is out front. There is a reason for this: Hawkins skillfully uses post-production as its own instrument, weaving musical elements together, splicing, looping, and layering them in unique ways, creating and composing something entirely new from these recordings. This technique is certainly nothing new; Teo Macero used a similar approach to create Bitches Brew (Columbia Records, 1970), but here Hawkins shows what it could sound like in the modern world of jazz, where the artist can pull elements from virtually anywhere and weave them into their sonic tapestry. Album opener, "Solo Way Far Gone," sets the tone immediately with its simple yet effective synth line, or is it a synth? We do not know, and that is the point! This is highly reminiscent of the trips through the spaceways that Sun Ra so often took us on. Elsewhere, on "Resolution Each and Every," Drake's beats take center stage, while the background is a whirlwind of sounds and instruments coming in and out of view in a game of sonic peekaboo. Ultimately, No Nation But Imagination succeeds because it takes the old jazz rulebook and throws it away. By not using traditional instruments like saxophone or piano to state the main theme and take the lead on these songs, Hawkins constructs a futuristic sonic world where anything is possible, and any preconceived notions disappear like tears in the rain. It is an exciting proposition and a bit of a radical viewpoint in the world of the avant-garde.

items.body: Babies On Airplanes is Anna Ueland's trio project. The cover's suggestion of a run-of-the-mill piano/synthesiser-bass-drums trio formula is deceptive. The album deploys a bric-à-brac in the service of a jazz that navigates between synth-pop, pure improvisation (whatever that means), rock, and pretty much anything else one might want to put in it. Ueland, a physicist who turned to music early, is a unique voice on the young Norwegian jazz scene, impressing through her vigorously melodic instinct (melody: first keyword), without any musical style being spared. In other circumstances, Ueland would contribute to a furious swing rooted as far back as Count Basie, as in Pauline Boty: bring her out! (Particular Recordings Collective, 2026) by Jenny frøysa's Artful Ensemble, released two months earlier; or to string music that defies words: Popular Music For Like-Minded People, for which an avatar is expected later in 2026. Music For A Noisy Environment balances six free improvisations and six compositions. Ueland's piano is rather in its flea-market incarnation, and readily gives way to the Wurlitzer. Through "Three Days in a Flow," "Monkey Brain," and "Kong Kokong" (where everyone takes to the piano) there floats the pleasant nostalgia of Jenny frøysa's Artful Ensemble the pianist. The drums of Gustav Tornberg are complemented by an array of light percussion that lifts the music, which Johannes Einan (bass) nevertheless anchors firmly in jazz tonality. Reverie ("Cassiopeja," "Riddles and Raccoons") is a second keyword. Ideas passing through the mind, atmospheres that emerge and follow one another in the noisy environment of intercontinental flights that Babies on Airplanes explore in a somewhat phantasmatic way ("Small Fish in a Big Pond"), while sparing us their carbon footprint. Ueland wanders a little through all corners with her out-of-tune piano, and the trio depicts these moments where everything and nothing happens: the clouds, perhaps a stretch of Greenland ("Transatlantic Scene"), a contrail, the irregular noise of a trolley. When the cabin lights go out, when one is not tired, or too tired; when even numbing oneself in front of a mindless film no longer appeals, what remains are the senses alert, thought more or less under control, a vaporous imagination catching the tiny things (or animals?) unfolding to the left and to the right. All this is in the album. A third keyword is cinematic. There is no need to bore yourself stiff on a plane. Everyone can make the album their own and script their day, preferably one of waiting or idleness. "Det var kjempebra (It was brilliant)!—Å ja! (Oh yes!)." (You can hear it at the end of the first track already, "Guro's tape.") A superb discovery indeed!
